plan.topic: Tirzepatide (Mounjaro/Zepbound) after 6 months: what to expect from month 6 onward. The rest of the SURMOUNT-1 average curve to 72 weeks, what the label says about side effects easing, cardiometabolic changes reported at 72 weeks (waist, blood pressure), what the SURMOUNT-1 3-year prediabetes follow-up shows about the longer term, and how attention shifts from losing weight to keeping muscle, labs and results (series part 3)
plan.angle: Working title: 'Tirzepatide (Zepbound/Mounjaro) After 6 Months: What the Big Trial Showed'. Opening: 'Six months into tirzepatide? In the big obesity trial, average weight loss kept going but slowed, and the focus shifts to keeping your results.' Chapter 2 title: 'Does the nausea keep easing?' Quote the label sentence exactly: 'The majority of nausea, vomiting, and/or diarrhea events occurred during dose escalation and decreased over time.' Cite the label edition actually used (DailyMed shows a 16 Nov 2026 revision). Chapter 4: frame the 3-year results as trial averages in adults with prediabetes plus obesity or overweight, and say that preventing diabetes is not an approved use. Everything else stays as briefed.

plan.why:
Playbook queue item 4 and series part 3. A searched what-to-expect format resting on settled label and SURMOUNT-1 evidence, with steady search and a New Year spike to come. | fact-check: Good evergreen topic: series part 3, a clear search question and strong evidence. These parts check out: the SURMOUNT-1 72-week results (Jastreboff, NEJM 2022) and the 3-year prediabetes analysis (Lancet, 176 weeks: 1.3% vs 13.3% developed type 2 diabetes, then 2.4% vs 13.7% after 17 weeks off treatment). Four fixes before scripting.
(1) The side-effect wording in the brief is wrong. The current Zepbound label on DailyMed (revised 16 Nov 2026, newer than the 28 Aug 2026 date in our notes) says: "The majority of nausea, vomiting, and/or diarrhea events occurred during dose escalation and decreased over time." Copy that sentence exactly. It only covers nausea, vomiting and diarrhea, so chapter 2 can't say side effects in general ease. Don't write 'mostly', and don't apply the sentence to constipation, hair loss or anything else. Cite the label edition the script actually uses, with its real revision date. Re-check the Table 2 numbers in that edition, because the hair-loss figure may have changed.
(2) Brand scope. SURMOUNT-1 is the obesity trial (adults without diabetes), which matches Zepbound's approved use. Mounjaro is approved for type 2 diabetes. A title that names only Mounjaro mislabels the data.
(3) Wording in the opening. 'Keeping what you've gained' is confusing in a weight-loss video. Use 'keeping your results'.
(4) The prediabetes chapter must say these are trial averages in people with prediabetes plus obesity or overweight, that preventing diabetes is not an approved use, and that 'developed type 2 diabetes' is the trial's measure. Never call it 'prevents diabetes'.
Keep the full DXA scope (160-person substudy, about 75% fat and 25% lean, lean mass isn't pure muscle), the kidney caveat on protein, and the line about never changing blood pressure medicines on your own. Before scripting, check the live list for overlap with Months 2–6, Plateau and How Long.

package.description:
If you have severe pain in your stomach area that will not go away, with or without vomiting, stop using tirzepatide and get medical help right away. For anything that isn't that emergency sign, don't stop or change your medicine on your own.

In SURMOUNT-1 (adults with obesity, or overweight plus a weight-related condition, without diabetes), average weight loss kept going after 6 months, just more slowly: about 15–21% across the three doses by week 72, versus about 3% on placebo.

The tirzepatide label: "The majority of nausea, vomiting, and/or diarrhea events occurred during dose escalation and decreased over time."

script.hook_pattern: Stakes + specificity, answer first: sentence 1 names tirzepatide, asks the month-six question and gives the trial answer (average loss kept going, more slowly). The headline number comes by about 11 s, and a one-sentence open loop about the 3-year blood sugar result pays off in chapter 6.

visual.stock_query: big number over gentle downhill graph

Zepbound is approved for adults with obesity, or overweight plus a weight-related condition, and for moderate to severe obstructive sleep apnea in adults with obesity. Mounjaro is the same medicine, approved for type two diabetes, with separate trials.

scenes.narration: So if your scale moves less than it did in month two, that slower pace fits the shape of the average curve.

visual.stock_query: relieved woman looking at gentle curve

scenes.retention_device: Relief fact tied to the viewer's lived moment

scenes.narration: From here, the focus shifts from losing weight to keeping your results: your muscle, your health numbers and your habits.
You will see how the curve bends, what the label says about nausea, and what changed besides the scale.
scenes.retention_device: Roadmap of what the viewer gets

scenes.narration: And stay for the three-year follow-up, where one blood sugar number stands out.
scenes.retention_device: Open loop, paid off in 'Three years later'

scenes.narration: Imagine Dana, fifty, six months into Zepbound. In month two, her scale dropped almost every week. Lately it barely moves, and she has started to wonder if something is wrong.

visual.stock_query: worried woman at scale, dark night bathroom

scenes.narration: First, the rest of the curve.
In SURMOUNT-1, the average tirzepatide curve dropped fastest in the early months, then kept falling at a gentler slope through week seventy-two.

visual.stock_query: line graph steep then gentle slope

scenes.retention_device: Answers the title question in depth

scenes.narration: Think of a hill that gets less steep: you are still heading down, just with smaller steps.

visual.stock_query: woman walking down gentle hill, smiling

scenes.narration: Here is a detail people miss: everyone in the trial, placebo group included, got counseling on a reduced-calorie diet and more physical activity.
So that three percent on placebo shows roughly what counseling plus placebo injections did, on average, in this trial.

visual.stat_label: Avg loss, placebo plus counseling, 72 weeks

scenes.narration: By week seventy-two, eighty-five to ninety-one percent across the tirzepatide doses had lost at least five percent of their weight, versus thirty-five percent on placebo.

visual.stock_query: crowd of people icons filling up

scenes.narration: And on the two higher doses, half or more lost at least twenty percent, versus three percent on placebo.
But averages hide a range: in every group, some people lost more than the average and some lost less.
So Dana's slower scale is not a verdict on her. If it stays flat for a long stretch, that is a conversation for her prescriber, not a reason to change anything herself.
But the scale is only half of what people wonder about at month six. The other half is the stomach.

visual.stock_query: curious Medi pointing at tummy icon

scenes.narration: So, does the nausea keep easing?
Nausea, vomiting and diarrhea are listed among the common adverse reactions on the tirzepatide label.

visual.stock_query: label page with three highlighted words

scenes.narration: And the label has one sentence on timing, word for word: 'The majority of nausea, vomiting, and/or diarrhea events occurred during dose escalation and decreased over time.'

visual.quote: The majority of nausea, vomiting, and/or diarrhea events occurred during dose escalation and decreased over time.
visual.attribution: Zepbound (tirzepatide) Prescribing Information, section 6.1, rev. 16 Nov 2026

scenes.narration: Dose escalation means the weeks when the dose is being stepped up, on the schedule your prescriber sets.

visual.stock_query: staircase with calendar weeks, doctor nearby

scenes.narration: So for those three symptoms, the majority of events came during the step-up period, and then decreased over time.
One honest limit: that sentence covers nausea, vomiting and diarrhea only. It does not say constipation, hair loss or anything else eases the same way.

visual.myth: The label says every side effect fades
visual.fact: That sentence covers nausea, vomiting and diarrhea only

scenes.narration: Two habits that can help with nausea: eat smaller, more frequent meals, and take regular sips of a cold drink, unless you have been told to limit fluids.

items: Regular sips of a cold drink
visual.stock_query: small plate and cold drink, cosy kitchen

scenes.narration: One sign never waits. If you have severe pain in your stomach area that will not go away, with or without vomiting, stop using tirzepatide and get medical help right away.
scenes.on_screen_text: Severe pain in your stomach area that won't go away, with or without vomiting? Stop tirzepatide and get medical help right away

visual.stock_query: Medi calmly holding phone, help sign

scenes.retention_device: Safety beat (mid-chapter, not the chapter end)

scenes.narration: For anything that isn't that emergency sign, don't stop or change your medicine on your own.
For Dana, that sentence brings some relief: in the label's data, those three symptoms decreased over time.

visual.stock_query: Dana relaxing with tea, evening lamp

scenes.narration: Meanwhile, under the surface, the trial measured changes the scale never shows.
scenes.retention_device: Re-hook: new open loop into the next chapter

scenes.narration: So what changed besides weight?

visual.stock_query: chapter card, tape measure and heart

scenes.narration: Start with waist size. In the trial, it shrank by roughly fourteen to eighteen and a half centimeters on average across the doses, versus about four centimeters on placebo.

visual.stat_label: Avg waist change, 72 weeks; placebo −4 cm

scenes.narration: That is roughly five and a half to seven inches, about the length of a smartphone.
So a tape measure can show progress in weeks when the scale is quiet. Measure the same spot, at the same time of day.
Blood pressure moved too. The top number, systolic, fell by about seven millimeters of mercury on average with tirzepatide, versus about one on placebo.

visual.stock_query: blood pressure cuff with happy heart

scenes.narration: If you take blood pressure medicine, never change it on your own. As your weight changes, your prescriber may want to recheck your readings.
Which raises the big question at month six: when weight comes off, what is it actually made of?
scenes.on_screen_text: What is the weight made of?

visual.stock_query: curious Dana, question mark over body outline

scenes.retention_device: Question to the viewer before the chapter change

scenes.narration: Next, keeping your muscle.
In a substudy of one hundred sixty people who had body-composition scans, about three quarters of the weight lost on tirzepatide was fat, and about one quarter was lean mass.

visual.stat_label: Fat vs lean of weight lost, 160-person substudy

scenes.narration: Lean mass is not pure muscle. It includes muscle, but also water, organs and other tissue that is not fat or bone.

visual.fact: Lean mass also includes water, organs and other tissue
visual.stock_query: body diagram with water drops, organs

scenes.narration: So the scans cannot say exactly how much muscle was lost. But protecting muscle is a smart goal from here, and you have two levers.
Lever one is strength training. The adult guideline is muscle-strengthening activity on two or more days a week, working all the major muscle groups.
Bands, body weight and machines all count. Start where you are, and ask your clinician first if you have a health condition.
Lever two is protein. Building each meal around a protein food, like eggs, fish, beans or yogurt, is a practical way to get it in when appetite is small.

visual.stock_query: plate with eggs, fish, beans, yogurt

scenes.narration: One caveat: if you have kidney disease, ask your doctor before increasing protein.

visual.stock_query: doctor and patient reviewing meal plan

scenes.narration: Muscle is one part of keeping your results. The other is the weight itself, and one trial tested what happens when treatment stops.

visual.stock_query: Medi opening a trial folder, curious

scenes.narration: Next, keeping your results.

Fourteen percent: that is how much weight people regained, on average, in the year after switching to placebo, following thirty-six weeks on tirzepatide, in the SURMOUNT-4 trial of adults with obesity, or overweight plus a weight-related condition, without diabetes.

visual.stat_label: Avg regain, 52 wks after switching to placebo (after 36 wks tirzepatide); adults with obesity/overweight, no diabetes
visual.stock_query: arrow bending back up on graph

scenes.narration: Even so, they stayed nine point nine percent below their starting weight on average.
Those who kept taking tirzepatide lost a further five and a half percent over the same year.

visual.stat_label: Further loss, continued tirzepatide, same 52 weeks

scenes.narration: In that trial, weight tended to come back when treatment stopped. So any decision about continuing is one to make with your prescriber, never on your own.
And keeping results may matter for more than weight. Remember that blood sugar number? Here it is.
scenes.retention_device: Callback to the open loop, payoff next

scenes.narration: Fast-forward three years.
One point three percent versus thirteen point three percent: that is how many developed type two diabetes over about three years, on tirzepatide versus placebo.

visual.stat_label: Developed type 2 diabetes, 176 weeks, vs placebo
visual.stock_query: two bars, one tiny, one tall

scenes.narration: These are trial averages in adults with prediabetes plus obesity or overweight, followed for one hundred seventy-six weeks. 'Developed type two diabetes' is the trial's own measure, and preventing diabetes is not an approved use of tirzepatide.

visual.stock_query: Medi with three careful note cards

scenes.narration: Put another way, that is roughly one person in seventy-five on tirzepatide, versus about one in seven or eight on placebo.

visual.stock_query: rows of people icons, few highlighted

scenes.narration: Average weight loss at that point was about twelve to twenty percent across the doses, versus about one percent on placebo.

visual.stat_label: Avg weight loss at 176 weeks; placebo 1%

scenes.narration: After seventeen weeks off treatment, the rates were two point four percent versus thirteen point seven percent, so the gap narrowed a little.

visual.stat_label: Type 2 diabetes after 17 weeks off treatment
visual.stock_query: two bars, small one growing slightly

scenes.narration: Still, it is a hopeful signal: in this trial, the benefits reached beyond the scale and held for years on treatment.
Back to Dana, and her worry that something is wrong.

visual.stock_query: chapter card, Dana at kitchen table

scenes.narration: Her slower scale fits the trial's average curve, which kept falling after month six, just more gently.

visual.stock_query: Dana smiling at gentle downhill graph

scenes.narration: Her early nausea fits the label's pattern too: the majority of those events came during the step-up weeks and decreased over time.
And in the trial, progress showed up beyond the scale: smaller waists and lower blood pressure, on average.

visual.stock_query: tape measure and happy heart icons

scenes.narration: So month six is not the finish line. It is the point where the goal shifts from losing faster to keeping your results.

visual.stock_query: Dana crossing a milestone marker, proud

scenes.narration: Imagine Dana a few weeks later: two short strength sessions a week, a protein food at every meal, and a tape measure next to the scale.
Here is your month-six checklist, in three steps.
One: track more than the scale. Your waist, your blood pressure and your lab results tell the fuller story, so note them alongside your weight.

visual.stock_query: notebook with waist and BP notes

scenes.narration: Two: protect your muscle, with strength work on two or more days a week and a protein food at every meal, keeping that kidney caveat in mind.
Three: bring your questions to your prescriber, from a long stall to a side effect that lingers, and never change a medicine on your own.

visual.stock_query: patient with question list at clinic

scenes.narration: If you have felt like a slower scale means you are failing, the trial data suggests a slower pace is simply part of this stage.

visual.stock_query: Medi giving Dana a warm high five

factcheck.summary:
The script is accurate and safe, so it passes. I've listed three small wording fixes below.

**Checked against the papers and labels:**
- **SURMOUNT-1 at 72 weeks:** weight loss of −15.0, −19.5 and −20.9% vs −3.1% on placebo. 85–91% lost at least 5% (vs 35%), and 50–57% on the two higher doses lost at least 20% (vs 3%).
- **SURMOUNT-1 waist, blood pressure and scans:** waist fell 14.0–18.5 cm vs 4.0 cm. Systolic blood pressure fell 7.2 vs 1.0 mmHg (pooled tirzepatide). The 160-person DXA substudy found roughly 3:1 fat to lean loss.
- **SURMOUNT-4:** +14.0% regain after switching to placebo, still 9.9% below starting weight, and −5.5% further loss on continued tirzepatide. The population is stated correctly.
- **176-week prediabetes analysis (NEJM 2025):** type 2 diabetes in 1.3% vs 13.3%, and 2.4% vs 13.7% after 17 weeks off treatment. Weight loss was −12.3% to −19.7% vs −1.3%. "About 1 in 75" and "1 in 7 or 8" are fair conversions.
- **Zepbound label on DailyMed:** revision date of 16 Nov 2026 confirmed. The section 6.1 sentence on nausea, vomiting and/or diarrhea is quoted word for word.
- **Mounjaro label:** confirmed as revised 11/2026. It also now lists children 10 and older and cardiovascular risk reduction in type 2 diabetes. The script's "approved for type two diabetes" is still accurate.
- **NHS nausea tips and the US activity guideline (strength work on 2 or more days a week):** match their sources.

**Safety:** all the needed caveats are there: don't change your medicine on your own, blood pressure medicine, kidney disease and protein, the fluid-limit exception, and diabetes prevention not being an approved use. Dana is clearly hypothetical and isn't shamed. The hook and title deliver what they promise.

**Minor fixes:**
1. s13 overstates "counseling alone": the placebo group also got placebo injections.
2. s26's on-screen card shortens the emergency wording.
3. s3 leaves out Zepbound's sleep apnea approval.

issues.claim: So that three percent on placebo shows roughly what counseling alone did, on average, in this trial.
issues.problem: The placebo group got counseling plus placebo injections, not counseling alone. "Counseling alone" slightly overstates what the trial isolated, and the scene's own stat label already says "placebo plus counseling".
issues.fix: Narration: "So that three percent on placebo shows roughly what counseling plus placebo injections did, on average, in this trial." On-screen text: "3% = placebo + counseling, roughly"

issues.claim: Severe stomach pain that won't go away? Stop tirzepatide, get medical help right away
issues.problem: The card shortens the spoken emergency line. It drops "area" and "with or without vomiting", which goes against the rule to copy the safety wording in full. The narration itself is correct.
issues.fix: On-screen text: "Severe pain in your stomach area that won't go away, with or without vomiting? Stop tirzepatide and get medical help right away"

issues.claim: Zepbound is approved for adults with obesity, or overweight plus a weight-related condition.
issues.problem: This is accurate but incomplete. The 16 Nov 2026 label also approves Zepbound for moderate to severe obstructive sleep apnea in adults with obesity. Not misleading, just partial.
issues.fix: Optional: "Zepbound is approved for adults with obesity, or overweight plus a weight-related condition, and for moderate to severe obstructive sleep apnea in adults with obesity."

thumbnail.reasoning:
All three candidates keep the curiosity gap open (none give away the trial's answer) and pair a worried/surprised face that matches the tone of the text, so none trip the hard caps. Legibility is strong across the board: short headlines in 2-3 words, bold sans-serif, clear single focal character, readable at phone size (240px and 168px).
